findings.title: Cleanup debug logs left at Error level and dump every ID
findings.body: CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags log every batch with r.log.Error, including the full ID slice, the SQL condition, and a nil err (same pattern at lines 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579). These run on the normal cleanup path, including the orphan-tag pass that always executes and the empty-batch case that happens when there is nothing to delete. Each scheduled cleanup will therefore emit error-level logs even when healthy, and when retention is configured a batch can be tens of thousands of IDs. That floods logs, inflates error metrics/alerts, and can stall or OOM the cleanup job while formatting the slice. These look like leftover diagnostics and should be removed or dropped to debug without the ID list.

findings.title: Cleanup scheduler interval accidentally reduced from 10 minutes to 1
findings.body: CleanUpService.Run now ticks every 1 minute instead of 10, and the PR does not mention this. clean() is synchronous and its context timeout is 9 minutes, so the old interval left a gap between runs. With a 1-minute ticker, any cleanup that lasts longer than a minute (the timeout allows up to 9) finds a tick already pending and starts the next pass immediately, so temporary-file, snapshot, dashboard-version, image, annotation, invite, short-URL, and query-history cleanup can run back-to-back. That is a large unintended load increase and is unrelated to the MySQL deadlock fix; restore the 10-minute interval.

findings.title: SQLite ID list is built with quadratic string concatenation
findings.body: When the database is SQLite and AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is above 999, deleteByIDs inlines every ID by repeatedly doing values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v). That copies the whole growing string on each ID. The new path is specifically for large batches (the test uses 32767, and the setting can be set higher), so one DELETE builds O(n^2) bytes of temporary strings — several seconds and heavy GC at 32k IDs, and much worse if the batch size is raised further. Build the list with strings.Builder (or strings.Join of preformatted IDs) instead.
